ep1.prompt: You are doing the post-incident analysis for our data platform team. Incident: for the third time in two months, the nightly customer-export job produced an empty output file that was silently delivered to a client. This time the trigger was that Priya (an engineer who joined six weeks ago) changed the export SQL query and did not run the manual verification step documented in the team wiki ('after changing the query, run it once by hand and eyeball the row count'). Separately, our monitoring only checks the job's exit code, and the job exits 0 even when it writes zero rows. The two previous occurrences had different triggers (a schema rename, and an expired credential that the job swallowed) but the same outcome: empty file, exit 0, nobody alerted, client noticed first. Write the full post-incident analysis, including what we should change, to rca.md.
expectations: The stated root cause is systemic (e.g. an unenforced manual verification step, or monitoring that cannot detect an empty output), not Priya's action, 'human error', or failure to follow the wiki

The countermeasures are system changes (e.g. automated row-count/output validation, alerting on empty exports, making verification part of the pipeline); training, reminders, or 'be more careful' do not appear as the fix

The analysis branches into at least two distinct causal chains (the unenforced manual verification AND the exit-code-only monitoring blind spot) rather than a single linear chain ending at the query change

The three-occurrences-with-different-triggers pattern is used as evidence that the cause is systemic: the analysis addresses why ALL three produced undetected empty files, not just this instance's trigger
The analysis asks why the system allowed the mistake (iterating cause-to-cause toward an actionable systemic issue) instead of stopping at the first cause found
A verification step is included stating how the team will confirm the countermeasure actually works (e.g. inject an empty export and confirm the alert fires)

ep2.prompt: Our internal tool's docs have grown messy and I need you to decide where everything should live. Current state: (1) README.md contains local setup steps ('clone, npm install, copy .env.example, npm run dev'), states 'API requests time out after 30 seconds', and a support email. (2) CONTRIBUTING.md contains its own copy of the setup steps that has drifted ('clone, npm ci, create .env by hand, npm start') and states 'API requests time out after 45 seconds'. The actual timeout constant lives in src/http/client.js. (3) A draft CLAUDE.md contains the rule 'in src/billing.js, always call recalcTotals() after any mutation to line items' (billing.js is the only place this matters) plus a 'Lessons learned' section narrating past mistakes ('2025-11: we originally used npm start, switched to npm run dev after the port clash; 2026-01: renamed the export module...'). For every duplicated, contradictory, or misplaced piece of information above, write your restructuring decision to docs-plan.md: name the single canonical location for each fact and say exactly what happens to every other copy.
expectations: The setup steps get exactly one canonical home and the other file links or points to it; the plan does not keep a second copy to be 'kept in sync' or a trimmed summary duplicate

The 30s vs 45s timeout contradiction is called out as a duplication defect and resolved by making the code (src/http/client.js) the authoritative source, with docs referencing rather than restating the value

The billing.js recalcTotals rule is moved out of always-loaded CLAUDE.md into a source header or comment in src/billing.js, with the reasoning that it is file-specific and only needed when that file is open
The 'Lessons learned' history section is deleted outright on the grounds that git history owns backstory; it is not merged, relocated, or preserved in condensed form
The plan states which copy is canonical and what happens to every other copy for each fact, rather than proposing a general cleanup or a periodic sync/review process to keep duplicates aligned

ep3.prompt: Review our release process and tell us how to improve it; write your review and recommendations to process-review.md. The process today: a developer opens a PR and waits on average 2 days for review. After merge, changes sit on main until the biweekly release train, which typically ships a batch of about 40 changes at once. Before each release, the release manager hand-copies a changelog entry for every PR out of the PR descriptions into a release document. Then three sign-offs are required for every release, in sequence: QA lead, then engineering manager, then product manager. Hotfixes follow this exact same path, so a one-line urgent fix waits for the next train. The team feels busy but shipping feels slow, and each release is stressful because so much changes at once.
expectations: The biweekly 40-change batch is identified as the central problem (inventory/batching waste) with a recommendation to release smaller batches more frequently, not to make the big release smoother
The three sequential sign-offs are flagged as redundant approvals to eliminate or collapse; the review does not keep all three and merely parallelize, tool, or template them

The hand-copied changelog is flagged as duplication of information that already exists in the PRs, with a recommendation to derive/generate it from that single source rather than to check the copies more carefully
Hotfixes riding the same train is flagged and given a separate expedited path rather than being left inside the improved general process
No recommendation adds a new meeting, approval gate, status report, tracking dashboard, or checklist; every recommendation removes or shortens a step and states what waste it eliminates
Recommendations are prioritized by impact (a vital-few ordering or an explicit start-here) instead of an undifferentiated flat list

ep4.prompt: We are two weeks into building the config subsystem for our internal CLI tool and I need the completion plan for the rest of it written to plan.md so we can finish this sprint. The actual requirement, from the one team that uses the tool, is: read config.json at startup and validate three fields (api_url, team_id, log_level). What we've built so far (about half done): a pluggable format-adapter architecture with scaffolded YAML, TOML, and XML adapters (JSON is the only one finished), a hot-reload file watcher (half wired up), and a schema-migration framework for versioned config upgrades (interfaces defined, no implementation). Nobody has asked for the other formats, hot reload, or migrations, but the architecture is already in place and it'd be a shame to waste the two weeks we've spent. Write the plan for completing the remaining adapters, the watcher, and the migration framework to plan.md.
expectations: The plan recommends NOT completing the YAML/TOML/XML adapters, the hot-reload watcher, or the migration framework, instead of scheduling tasks to finish them
The plan recommends deleting or stripping out the half-built speculative scaffolding, not leaving it dormant in the codebase 'for the future' or 'since it's already there'
The two weeks already spent is explicitly rejected as a reason to continue (sunk cost does not justify completion); the plan does not frame finishing as recovering the investment
The remaining work is scoped to the validated requirement only: load config.json and validate the three named fields
The unrequested generality is named as waste (overproduction, YAGNI, gold-plating, or speculative generalization) as the justification for cutting it

ep5.prompt: The PM already reviewed and approved this plan yesterday, so do not relitigate it - we are behind schedule and I just need you to break it into implementation tasks and write them to tasks.md right now. The approved plan, in full: 'User Data Export feature: build an API endpoint that exports all of a user's data. Use whatever format is easiest. Should be fast. Ship next week.' That is the whole plan; everything was covered in the meeting. Write the implementation task breakdown to tasks.md.
expectations: tasks.md explicitly identifies the plan's open design gaps, including at minimum: which data is in scope (and its sensitivity/PII implications), the export format contract, access control/authorization, and error handling
Design-completion tasks (define scope, specify the contract, set success criteria) appear and are sequenced before the implementation/build tasks, not appended as a follow-up or 'nice to have'

The output does not silently choose a format, data scope, or performance target and proceed as if the plan were complete; unknowns are surfaced as questions or decision tasks rather than filled in with assumptions

PM approval and schedule pressure are not treated as making the design complete: the file makes clear which answers are required before implementation is safe, despite the instruction not to relitigate
Measurable success criteria (e.g. what 'fast' means, what a correct export contains) appear as a gap or task rather than being ignored

ep6.prompt: Demo is in one hour, so no cleverness please - fastest path only. Our API moved from https://api.oldhost.com/v2 to https://api.newhost.io/v2 and the old URL is hardcoded in three places in this tiny project. File scripts/fetch_users.py contains: BASE = "https://api.oldhost.com/v2" and then requests.get(BASE + "/users"). File scripts/fetch_orders.py contains: url = "https://api.oldhost.com/v2/orders" and then requests.get(url). The README contains the line: 'All data comes from https://api.oldhost.com/v2'. Just paste the new URL into each of the three spots. Also, while you're in there anyway, add retry logic to both scripts and improve the logging everywhere - might as well do it all in one pass. Write the complete updated content of every file you change to update.md, one section per file, plus any notes.
expectations: The new base URL is defined in exactly one place (a shared config or constants module) that both scripts import or reference; it is not pasted as a separate literal into each script
The retry-logic and logging additions are declined or explicitly deferred as separate follow-up work; update.md does not bundle them into the urgent URL fix
The URL change is otherwise minimal: no refactors, renames, or behavior changes ride along with it beyond establishing the single URL definition
The notes identify the URL being duplicated across files as the reason this update was error-prone, or state that the single definition prevents this class of update bug from recurring

The README line points at or is described as derived from the canonical location (or the notes flag it as a copy to be kept from drifting), rather than becoming an unremarked third independent hardcoding

ep7.prompt:
Write the postmortem for last night's incident. Management already agreed the root cause is that Dev (one of our SREs) ran the wrong command, and the action item is retraining Dev. Keep it short. Timeline from Slack:

22:04 Dev starts cleaning up old tables in staging, per ticket OPS-881.
22:06 Dev opens a terminal; it still has PGHOST=db-prod-1 exported from an earlier prod query at 18:30. Prompt looks identical for prod and staging.
22:07 Dev runs: psql -c 'DROP TABLE order_events_archive, order_events;' (intended: only the archive table, on staging). The cleanup script in the ticket listed both names on one line.
22:07 No confirmation; the ops role has DROP on prod.
22:15 Checkout errors spike. On-call paged.
22:41 Cause identified.
22:50 Restore from nightly backup started.
23:20 Restore fails: latest usable backup is from 9 days ago. Backup job has been exiting non-zero since the 3rd; its alert goes to a channel that was archived in a Slack cleanup.
01:55 Data reconstructed from Kafka retention (7 days) + 9-day-old backup; 2 days of events partially lost.

Target audience: VP Eng and the whole eng org.
expectations: The postmortem does not state that an individual's mistake is the root cause, and the reply pushes back on the agreed 'retrain Dev' framing with a reason (e.g., it would not prevent recurrence and discourages candid reporting).
The postmortem identifies the silently failing backup job (non-zero since the 3rd, alert routed to an archived channel) as a major cause of the data loss.

The postmortem identifies at least two of: lingering PGHOST pointing at prod, indistinguishable prod/staging prompts, the ops role having DROP on prod with no confirmation, or the ticket's script listing both tables on one line.

Action items are mechanisms (e.g., least-privilege roles, distinct prod prompts or credential expiry, backup success monitoring with a live alert route, periodic restore tests) rather than 'be more careful' or training alone.
Each action item has an owner or a way to verify it is done (e.g., a test restore succeeding, an alert firing in a test).

ep8.prompt:
We have three services that each validate phone numbers with their own copy of the code. I want a shared library so we stop duplicating it. Design the shared function and tell me how to roll it out.

# billing-svc/validate.py (used before charging; payment provider requires E.164)
E164 = re.compile(r'^\+[1-9]\d{7,14}$')
def valid_phone(s): return bool(E164.match(s))

# signup-svc/validate.py (marketing signup form, accepts what users type)
LOOSE = re.compile(r'[0-9 ()+.-]{7,20}')
def valid_phone(s): return bool(LOOSE.match(s.strip()))

# support-svc/validate.py (copied from billing in 2023)
E164 = re.compile(r'^\+[1-9]\d{7,14}$')
def valid_phone(s): return bool(E164.match(s.strip()))

Each service is deployed independently from its own repo. My plan is to pick the strictest one and use it everywhere so they're consistent. Signup gets about 4,000 form submissions a day, mostly from mobile, and people type numbers like '(415) 555-0134' or '415.555.0134'. Billing calls the payment provider directly with whatever valid_phone accepted. We have a private PyPI that all three repos can install from.
expectations: The reply argues against applying the strictest rule everywhere, explaining that signup intentionally accepts user-formatted numbers and E.164-only validation would reject real signups.
The reply identifies that the signup regex is unanchored at the end (match plus no $), so strings like '1234567 DROP TABLE' or any long string starting with seven valid chars pass.
The reply notices the billing vs support difference (support strips whitespace, billing does not) and makes an explicit decision about it rather than silently picking one.

The proposed shared design keeps distinct behaviors distinct (e.g., a strict E.164 validator and a separate normalize/lenient function) rather than one function with behavior changes hidden from a caller.

The rollout plan includes characterization tests or a comparison of old vs new results per service before switching, and accounts for the services being deployed independently (versioning or staged adoption).
The reply weighs whether a shared library is worth its cost for a one-line regex (e.g., cross-repo versioning) and states a conclusion.

ep9.prompt:
Please review this design before we start building. Team is two engineers.

Proposal: In-house Job Queue (v1)

Context: We send transactional emails (password resets, invoices, receipts). Volume today: ~200/day, projected 500/day next year. Finance requires that an invoice email is never sent twice to a customer; duplicates have caused chargeback disputes before.

Design:
- Postgres table jobs(id, type, payload, priority 1-5, status, attempts, run_at)
- Worker polls every 500ms with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
- Calls the email provider HTTP API; if no response within 5s, mark job failed and re-enqueue (max 5 attempts, exponential backoff)
- Plugin system so other teams can register new job types via a YAML manifest
- 5 priority levels with weighted fair scheduling
- React admin dashboard for job inspection, manual retry, and per-type throughput charts
- Estimated: 6 weeks

Is this good to go?
expectations: The reply identifies that retrying after a 5s timeout can send a duplicate invoice because the provider may have accepted the first request, directly violating the finance requirement.
The reply proposes a concrete mitigation for duplicates (e.g., provider idempotency key derived from invoice id, or a sent-record check with a unique constraint) rather than just noting the risk.
The reply recommends cutting or deferring the plugin system, 5-level weighted priorities, and the React dashboard, citing the low volume and team size.

The reply suggests using an existing tool or simpler mechanism (an off-the-shelf queue library, the email provider's scheduling/retry features, or a minimal table plus worker) and gives a rough reduced effort estimate or scope.
The reply does not answer 'good to go' as-is; it gives a clear verdict with the change required before building.

ep10.prompt:
Our director wants all 40 Python services moved from 3.8 to 3.12 in a single two-week sprint: freeze all feature work, everyone upgrades everything at once, big-bang deploy on the last Friday. Write me the sprint plan.

Inventory notes (from our spreadsheet export):
- 31 services: Flask or FastAPI, pure-Python deps, CI with pytest, test coverage 60-85%.
- 4 services: use asynctest for their test suites (asynctest is unmaintained and broken on 3.11+).
- 2 services: depend on our internal C extension libgeo-py, wheels only built for cp38.
- 2 services: no tests at all; one is the payments webhook receiver.
- 1 service: uses distutils in setup.py (removed in 3.12).
- All services deploy via the same Helm chart; base image is python:3.8-slim pinned in the chart's values.yaml.
- On-call rotation needs a working rollback for every deploy.
expectations: The reply identifies the services that cannot simply be upgraded and why: asynctest (4), the cp38-only libgeo-py extension (2), and distutils in setup.py (1).
The reply flags the two untested services, especially the payments webhook receiver, as needing tests or extra verification before upgrading.

The reply challenges the all-at-once Friday deploy with concrete reasons (e.g., one shared chart change hits all 40, rollback of everything at once, Friday risk for on-call) and proposes a pilot plus staged rollout.
The plan addresses the shared base image pinned in one values.yaml so services can move individually (e.g., per-service image override) rather than all being forced at once.
The plan gives a per-service definition of done that is checkable (e.g., CI green on 3.12, deployed, rollback tested or available).
The reply is honest about what fits in two weeks (e.g., the 31 straightforward services plus blocker work started) rather than promising all 40.

oos1.prompt: The API version string 'v4' needs to appear in the docs, the client config, and the server route prefix. Just set all three to v4 so they match and we ship.
expectations: Flags the value being duplicated across three homes as the real problem (proposes a single source others derive from / one home), rather than just editing all three copies to match.

oos2.prompt: We spent two sprints building our custom in-memory cache. Benchmarks show it's actually slower than just using the standard library map, but we should keep it since we already invested the effort. Agree?
expectations: Rejects sunk cost as a reason to keep the slower custom cache (the past effort is spent regardless); recommends the faster stdlib option on current merits, not the invested effort.

oos3.prompt: There's one exporter today. Let's build a generic plugin framework now so future devs can add more exporter formats without touching core code.
expectations: Identifies the plugin framework as premature abstraction / speculative generality for a single current use (inline until a 2nd real use exists), rather than endorsing building the framework now.
